intro.title: Build permissions utility can action subject
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a permissions utility function called 'can' that checks if a user is allowed to perform a specific action on a subject. You'll learn how to implement conditional logic to compare user permissions against required actions. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, objects, and comparison operators. This beginner-friendly project will help you understand how to structure and use utility functions for access control in applications.
intro.usecase: Permission utilities like 'can(action, subject)' are essential in any application with user roles and access control. You'll see this pattern in admin dashboards where different users can view, edit, or delete content based on their permissions. For example, in a project management tool, a team member might only 'view' tasks while a manager can 'edit' or 'delete' them. Similarly, e-commerce admin panels use such utilities to control who can 'manage' products, 'process' orders, or 'view' customer data. Implementing this utility helps you build secure, role-aware interfaces that prevent unauthorized actions.

objectives: Implement a permissions utility function that checks user actions on subjects
Construct a role-based permission structure using JavaScript objects
Apply conditional logic to evaluate user permissions against requested actions
Initialize permission configurations for different user roles and resources
Manipulate permission data structures to add or modify access rules
Integrate the permissions utility into a simple user interface component
Configure permission checks for multiple action-subject combinations

steps.title: Create the permissions utility function
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'can' that takes three parameters: action, subject, and permissions.
steps.hint: Start by writing a function declaration or arrow function with the name 'can' and three parameters in parentheses.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named 'can' is declared with three parameters: action, subject, and permissions.
successCriteria: The code contains a function named 'can' with three parameters (action, subject, permissions).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is named exactly 'can' and accepts all three parameters: action, subject, and permissions.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function wasn't created correctly. Please create a function named 'can' that takes three parameters: action, subject, and permissions.

steps.title: Add basic function structure and return false
steps.instruction: Inside your 'can' function, add a function body that returns the boolean value false.
steps.hint: Remember to use the return keyword followed by false.
steps.expectedOutcome: The 'can' function will have a body that returns false when called.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function returns the boolean value false.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function should return the boolean value false. Check your syntax and the return statement.

steps.title: Check if permissions object exists
steps.instruction: Inside your 'can' function, add a guard clause at the beginning that returns false if the 'permissions' parameter is falsy.
steps.hint: You can check if 'permissions' is falsy with a simple if statement. Remember to place this check before any other logic in the function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function will immediately return false when no permissions object is provided, preventing errors when trying to access properties on undefined.
successCriteria: The 'can' function contains an if statement that checks if 'permissions' is falsy and returns false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your guard clause checks the 'permissions' parameter and returns false when it's falsy.
steps.feedbackWrong: The guard clause is missing or incorrect. Add an if statement at the beginning of the function that returns false when 'permissions' is falsy.

steps.title: Access the subject permissions
steps.instruction: Inside the 'can' function, after the guard clause, access the 'subject' property from the permissions object and store it in a variable named 'subjectPermissions'.
steps.hint: Use dot notation or bracket notation to get the 'subject' property from the permissions parameter.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function will have a variable 'subjectPermissions' that holds the value of permissions.subject.
successCriteria: The 'subjectPermissions' variable is declared and assigned the value of permissions.subject.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're accessing the 'subject' property from the permissions parameter and storing it in a variable named 'subjectPermissions'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're correctly accessing the 'subject' property from the permissions object and storing it in a variable named 'subjectPermissions'.

steps.title: Check for wildcard permission
steps.instruction: Inside the can function, after checking if subjectPermissions exists, add a condition to check if the subjectPermissions array includes the wildcard character '*'. If it does, return true.
steps.hint: Use the includes() method on the subjectPermissions array to check for '*'. Place this check before the existing return false statement.
steps.expectedOutcome: The can function will now return true when the subject permissions include the wildcard character '*', before falling back to returning false.
successCriteria: The can function includes a condition that checks if subjectPermissions includes '*' and returns true when found.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking if subjectPermissions includes '*', and returning true when it does. Remember to place this check after verifying subjectPermissions exists.
steps.feedbackWrong: The wildcard permission check isn't working correctly. You need to check if subjectPermissions includes '*', and if it does, return true. This should happen before the final return false statement.

steps.title: Check for specific action permission
steps.instruction: Inside the can function, after checking for wildcard permission, add a check to see if the subject permissions include the specific action parameter.
steps.hint: You'll need to add a third parameter 'action' to the function signature, then check if subjectPermissions includes that action using the includes() method.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function will have the logic to check if the subject permissions array includes the specific action.
successCriteria: The can function has a third parameter 'action' and checks if subjectPermissions includes that action.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added the action parameter and used includes() to check if subjectPermissions contains it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function should have three parameters and check if subjectPermissions includes the action.

steps.title: Return the permission check result
steps.instruction: Update the function to return true if the action is found in the subject permissions, otherwise return false.
steps.hint: After checking for the wildcard and specific action, you need to return a boolean value based on whether the action was found.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function should return true when the action is permitted, and false otherwise.
successCriteria: Function returns true when action is found in subject permissions
Function returns false when action is not found
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're returning the correct boolean value based on whether the action was found.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't returning the correct boolean value. Check your conditional logic for the action permission check.

steps.title: Create test data for the utility
steps.instruction: Create a sample permissions object with different subjects and actions to test your utility function.
steps.hint: Define a variable (like 'samplePermissions') that contains an object with subjects as keys and arrays of allowed actions as values.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a sample permissions object ready to test your utility function.
successCriteria: A sample permissions object is defined with at least two subjects and different action arrays.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started creating the object, but make sure it has at least two subjects with different action arrays.
steps.feedbackWrong: The sample permissions object is missing or incomplete. Create an object with subjects as keys and arrays of allowed actions as values.

steps.title: Test the utility function with different cases
steps.instruction: Call the can function three times with different test cases to verify it works correctly. Write console.log statements to output the results.
steps.hint: Use the sample permissions object you created earlier and call can(permissions, subject, action) with different subjects and actions.
steps.analogousExample:
// Testing a function with different inputs
console.log(isEven(2)); // true
console.log(isEven(3)); // false
console.log(isEven(0)); // true
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll see three console.log outputs showing true/false results for different permission checks.
successCriteria: Three console.log statements call the can function with different subjects and actions, using the sample permissions object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some test cases, but try to include three different calls to the can function with varying subjects and actions.
steps.feedbackWrong: Make sure you're calling the can function with three different test cases and logging the results with console.log.
